questions.q: What does pessimistic concurrency assume, and how does it respond?
options: Conflicts are likely; it blocks other sessions up front to prevent them
Conflicts are rare; it lets everyone proceed and checks for conflicts only at write time
Conflicts never happen; it takes no precautions at all
Conflicts are a client-side problem the database ignores entirely
questions.explain: Pessimistic concurrency -- READ UNCOMMITTED through SERIALIZABLE -- uses locks to physically block other sessions before a conflict can occur.

questions.q: Which isolation levels are pessimistic, and which are optimistic?
options: READ UNCOMMITTED through SERIALIZABLE are pessimistic; SNAPSHOT and RCSI are optimistic
All six isolation levels are pessimistic
SNAPSHOT and SERIALIZABLE are pessimistic; the rest are optimistic
All six isolation levels are optimistic
questions.explain: The four ANSI locking-based levels assume conflicts are likely and block; SNAPSHOT and RCSI use row versioning and assume conflicts are rare.

questions.q: How does SNAPSHOT isolation illustrate the optimistic approach?
options: It never blocks a reader or writer, and only deals with a conflict (error 3960) after the fact, if one genuinely occurs
It blocks every writer until all readers finish
It prevents all possible conflicts before they can occur, like SERIALIZABLE
It disables concurrent access to a table entirely
questions.explain: SNAPSHOT lets every transaction proceed without blocking, and only raises an error when an actual write-write conflict happens at commit time.

questions.q: In the ROWVERSION example, what happens to the conditional UPDATE if another session already changed the row in between?
options: The UPDATE affects 0 rows, because the RowVer value no longer matches, signaling the application to reload and retry
The UPDATE succeeds anyway, silently overwriting the other session's change
SQL Server raises error 3960, the same as a SNAPSHOT write-write conflict
The UPDATE blocks until the row becomes available again
questions.explain: Because the WHERE clause includes the old RowVer value, a row that has since changed its RowVer simply won't match, so the UPDATE silently affects zero rows -- the application detects this via @@ROWCOUNT.

questions.q: What is the main cost of the optimistic approach when conflicts turn out to be frequent?
options: Frequent retries and wasted work, since conflicts are only detected after the fact
Permanent data corruption with no way to detect it
The database refuses to accept any writes at all
All sessions are forced into SERIALIZABLE mode automatically
questions.explain: Optimistic concurrency is cheap when conflicts are rare, but if conflicts are actually frequent, the cost shifts to repeated retries and discarded work.
